title: Two-sample inference for sequence-derived feature distributions from deep sequencing data
summary: Many biological contexts involve heterogeneous populations of related molecular variants within a single individual. For example, some viral infections such as HIV-1 exhibit substantial diversity within a single host. Advances in sequencing technology now make it possible to characterize such populations by generating up to thousands of genetic sequences from a biological sample. In many settings, each sequence can be mapped to a numeric feature, such as Hamming distance to a reference sequence. This collection of feature values defines a one-dimensional distribution that characterizes individual-level viral diversity. When comparing these features across independent groups, past analyses have typically reduced each individual's data to a single summary value, such as the mean or mode. We propose a framework that retains the full individual-level distribution as the object of analysis. Drawing on existing tools from distributional data analysis, our framework uses Wasserstein barycenters to summarize the observed individual-level distributions within groups into a single representative distribution. These group barycenters are then compared using differences in quantiles and tested for equality. A practical challenge is that the number of sequences obtained, known as sequencing depth, can vary across biological samples. Through simulation studies, we examine when low sequencing depth can distort inference and present practical strategies for addressing these issues. We then illustrate the framework using data from the HIV-1 Antibody Mediated Prevention efficacy trials and a human B cell receptor sequencing study of vaccine-elicited immune responses. By using the entire collection of sequences for each individual, our approach can reveal group differences that may be obscured by single-number summary analyses.

title: Close Races and Similarity Bias: A Bayesian Analysis of the Ranked Ballots for the Ballon d'Or
summary: The Ballon d'Or ranks players whose contributions have no common unit, so its results are often disputed. Regressions of award points describe associations but not how complete ballots arise or how likely a different winner would be. We propose a Bayesian mixture-of-experts model for partial rankings that learns nonlinear performance relationships, the number of voting styles and journalists' style memberships. A shared soft regression tree with style-specific leaf values lets styles evaluate the same season records differently on a common basis. Region-dependent mixing probabilities and journalist--nominee similarity terms separate geographic differences in voting styles from affinity within a style, and journalist- and rank-specific precisions capture remaining variation. We establish identification and consistency for the number of occupied styles under explicit conditions; simulations examine recovery, calibration and robustness to misspecification. Applied to all 176 published ballots from 2019 and 99 from 2024, the model compares award outcomes under changes in affinity and jury composition. For 2019, Messi's probability of winning with a new jury from the same countries rises from 0.49 to 0.76 when similarity terms are removed. For 2024, the direction of this change depends on whether affinities differ by region. Regional representation changes winner probabilities more than jury size.

title: Intrinsic Information-Theoretic Analysis of ReLU Nets
summary: Mutual information (MI) is fundamental to representation-learning analysis in deep networks, but in high dimensions MI estimators depend on hyperparameters whose bias often dominates the signal. We show that continuous piecewise-linear (CPWL) networks, including ReLU networks, admit an intrinsic information-theoretic analysis that avoids this pitfall: their inherent partition of the input space into convex linear regions assigns to every input a discrete region label $Π$ alongside the continuous representation $T$ and label $Y$. We introduce a decomposition of the mutual information $I(Y;T)$ into interpretable geometric terms. We show that the dominant term, the *routing information* $I(Y; Π)$, admits an estimable plug-in estimator, that in the well-sampled regime, approximates a population lower bound on the joint information $I(Y; Π, T)$. When the partition saturates, a functional-equivalence quotient collapses regions implementing the same linear operator and restores informativeness; this extension has a single bounded, dimensionless parameter, which is reported through the quotient's compression ratio. The routing estimator agrees strongly with three established MI baselines applied to the same networks and data. The functional quotient recovers informative estimates in the regime bordering the well-sampled and under-sampled regime. We provide a framework for analysing the internal information geometry of CPWL networks, grounded in their inherent piecewise-linear structure rather than in external discretisation.

title: Second-order Sinkhorn Geometry and $\sqrt{n}$-Inference
summary: The Sinkhorn divergence, a debiased form of entropic optimal transport, has been widely used in various scientific disciplines due to its computational and statistical tractability. Unlike the Wasserstein distance, however, the Sinkhorn divergence is not a metric and it does not naturally admit a formal Riemannian structure. These properties are central to many applications of optimal transport methods that utilize interpolation, barycentric averaging, parallel transport or other geometric operations. Recent work addresses these shortcomings by constructing a formal Riemannian tangent space and a metric tensor on the space of probability measures that quadratically approximates the Sinkhorn divergence. In this work, we extend this framework with two major threads of contributions. For a suitable class of finite-smoothness cost functions, we prove Hadamard differentiability of the Sinkhorn metric tensor and we derive the Levi-Civita covariant derivative in this geometry; we then use the covariant derivative to obtain the geodesic and parallel transport equations, each of which amount to an ODE on a fixed Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) with smooth coefficients. Our second contribution is to linearize the solutions to the geodesic and parallel transport equations using standard tools from Banach space ODE theory. We show that under standard regularity conditions these linearizations imply $\sqrt{n}$-limiting Gaussian processes centered at population values for the plugin estimators of the exponential map, the logarithmic map, parallel transport and the induced Sinkhorn distance. Moreover, we show that the nonparametric bootstrap is consistent for all objects mentioned. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first $\sqrt{n}$--limit theorems and bootstrap consistency results for canonical geometric operations in a transport-based geometry on the space of probability measures.

title: Effect-Size Estimation and Confounding-Aware Permutations for PERMANOVA
summary: Motivation: PERMANOVA is widely used to test associations between covariates and high-dimensional data with arbitrary distributions, such as ecology, metabolomics, or microbial community profiling. In these contexts, its effect size measure (R2) is generally used to indicate how much the high-dimensional measurement covaries with respect to a separate, univariate measure. However, as we show, this conventional effect size is inflated under the null, resulting in values that do not accurately reflect the conventional expectation of "variance explained." Furthermore, standard permutation schemes yield inflated false positives in the presence of non-independent samples, such as repeated measure designs. Results: We introduce confounding-aware permutation schemes for both invariant and variant covariates. We additionally develop a causally-grounded, distance-based effect-size estimator derived from the Hájek average treatment effect estimator, providing interpretable effect sizes in the units of the chosen dissimilarity metric. Simulations using microbiome profiles demonstrate that these approaches control false positives while maintaining power, outperforming standard PERMANOVA implementations. Availability and Implementation: An R implementation is freely available in the permaBrioche module of the bioBakery ecosystem https://huttenhower.sph.harvard.edu/permabrioche. Contact: chuttenh@hsph.harvard.edu

title: Relaxed MEMs: Enhancing Borrowing in Multisource Exchangeability Models for Small Sample Applications
summary: Information sharing in clinical trials provides a promising way to increase trial efficiency, specifically in rare disease settings where sample sizes are small. Multisource Exchangeability Modeling (MEM) is a method that incorporates historical data from potentially multiple data sources, such as past trials, by exploring all possible configurations of exchangeability and provides a weight estimate for each configuration, allowing the user to quantify how much is being borrowed from each source. While MEMs have previously been shown to be asymptotically consistent, small sample sizes introduce uncertainty that naturally limits the amount of borrowing MEMs can facilitate. The proposed ``relaxed MEMs'' provide a mathematical framework for relaxing or removing those limits and allowing greater borrowing even in small-sample settings. Several relaxed MEM versions are proposed, and all strategies provide enhanced borrowing with minimal sacrifice in the bias and variance of the mean estimates. Specifically, the maximum absolute mean bias was 3.5\% (0.035) of the true mean in the two source continuous outcome settings and 6.4\% (0.032) of the true proportion in the two source binary outcome settings (absolute mean bias was 1.4\% (0.014) and 3.6\% (0.018), respectively, for traditional MEMs) and variance decreased relative to traditional MEMs across all exchangeable and small difference scenarios. The methods were then demonstrated using two endpoints from a series of phase II trials in cystic fibrosis.

title: Doubly Robust Deep Kernel Tests for Structured Outcomes
summary: We propose a test of whether two interventions induce the same outcome distribution when outcomes are structured and high-dimensional, such as images, text and graphs. We represent the interventional distributions as mean embeddings on learned deep features, such that the treatment effect is a doubly robust representation of the difference in mean embeddings. Our test, DR-KTE-Deep, optimises the learned features so as to maximise an estimated power criterion on this treatment effect representation. To motivate our learning objective, we show that the power criterion characterises the asymptotic signal-to-noise ratio of the test under fixed alternatives, and we derive a uniform finite-sample bound for its regularised estimate. We show that, with the learned kernel fixed, a held-out test is asymptotically valid under the null given suitable nuisance-estimation rates. Empirically, DR-KTE-Deep achieves substantially higher power than fixed and bandwidth-optimised kernel baselines across image, text and graph outcomes, while maintaining well-calibrated Type-I error.

title: Coupled unbiased MCMC for estimating Shapley effects under dependent inputs
comment: 25 pages plus 6 pages of supplementary material; 2 figures in total
summary: In global sensitivity analysis, Shapley effects provide a game-theoretic allocation of output variance among potentially dependent inputs. Their computation typically requires repeated conditional sampling, which can be challenging even when independent samples from the joint input distribution can be generated exactly. This difficulty arises naturally in hierarchical models, where conditioning on arbitrary subsets need not follow the generative order. To efficiently estimate Shapley effects under such dependence between input variables, we propose a permutation-based framework using coupled unbiased Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). Our proposed method combines two complementary coupling mechanisms: (i) a joint coupling of conditional distributions along a random permutation, designed to reduce the variance of estimated marginal contributions, and (ii) a meeting-based coupling of Markov chains that removes finite-time MCMC bias through a telescoping correction. Under suitable conditions, we prove that the resulting estimators for the unnormalized Shapley effects are unbiased, and have finite variance and finite expected computational cost. Numerical experiments with various test cases illustrate the computational efficiency of the proposed method.

title: Contextual Factors Behind Income Inequality: A Predictive Analysis
summary:
Income inequality remains a central concern in economics and public policy, yet conclusions about its predictors often depend on both the factors considered and the measure of inequality used. This paper examines the predictive importance of a broad set of indicators covering structural factors, capital structure, financial-sector development, political institutions, regional classification, human capital, globalization, and technology. Using data for 88 countries from 1970 to 2017 and six inequality measures from the World Income Inequality Database (WIID), we apply a machine learning approach to assess the relative predictive importance of 35 candidate indicators across alternative income inequality measures.
  The analysis proceeds in three stages: a full specification including all candidate indicators, a category-representative specification with one common indicator from each conceptual category, and an inequality-specific specification allowing the most predictive indicator within each category to vary across inequality measures.
  Regional classification is the dominant predictor across all specifications and inequality measures, although its broad nature prevents identification of the specific regional characteristics underlying this result. Political and technology indicators provide the most consistent additional predictive information, whereas the importance of human capital, financial development, and globalization varies across inequality measures. Technology is particularly informative for top-income concentration, while returns to capital are more relevant for measures capturing gaps between the upper and lower parts of the income distribution.

title: Low-degree polynomials lower bounds for clustering in small dimension
summary: We study the computational limits of clustering $n$ observations drawn from a mixture of $K$ isotropic distributions in $\mathbb R^d$, in the regime where the number $K$ of groups is much larger than the dimension $d$. In this regime, tensor-based procedures recover the partition with a polylogarithmic separation between the centers, but they require a sample size that is a large and non-explicit polynomial of $dK$, whereas the existing low-degree lower bounds only show that $n$ must be larger than $dK^2$. We introduce a mixture of $2K$ product Bernoulli distributions on $\{0,1\}^d$, with $K=(d+1)^m$, whose centers are built from a dual BCH code. This construction ensures that the moment tensors of the observations coincide with those of the uniform distribution on $\{-1,1\}^d$ up to the order $2m+1$. For any fixed $m$, we establish a low-degree polynomial lower bound showing that clustering is hard as long as the separation $Δ$ satisfies $Δ^2\ll(K^2d^{3/2}/n)^{1/(2m+2)}\wedge\sqrt d$, up to polylogarithmic factors. In particular, with a polylogarithmic separation, low-degree polynomials require $n\gtrsim K^2d^{3/2}$ observations, up to polylogarithmic factors. Through a Gaussianization argument, this hardness carries over, in the sense of reductions, to isotropic Gaussian mixtures. Our proof relies on a family of polynomials of the observations, indexed by bipartite graphs, which is almost orthonormal. The moments of these polynomials are governed by the number of solutions of polynomial systems over the finite field $\mathbb F\_{d+1}$ that are induced by the BCH code, and the crux of our analysis is to connect the combinatorial structure of the bipartite graphs with the structure of the solution sets of these systems.

title: Robust Log-Contrast Regression for High-Dimensional Compositional Microbiome Data with Outliers
summary: It is well known that microbiome sequencing data are naturally compositional and often have a complex subcomposition structure, as well as a lot of noise and some outliers. These characteristics make classical log-contrast regression difficult to apply, because it is sensitive to extreme values and cannot fully meet the linear constraints of compositional predictors. To tackle these issues, in this paper, we propose a robust log-contrast regression framework that incorporates the Huber loss function along with a Lasso penalty, which not only boosts resistance to outliers but also facilitates sparse variable selection. It is important to note that the general linear constraints, which are explicitly imposed, serve to preserve the algebraic coherence of compositional and subcompositional covariates. Under some mild assumptions, we theoretically prove that the proposed method achieves non-asymptotic guarantees in finite samples, comparable to those of Huber loss estimators, ensuring robustness. To implement the method efficiently, we develop a symmetric Gauss--Seidel-based alternating direction method of multipliers based on its dual formulation with a convergence guarantee, and it is also easy to implement in the sense that each subproblem admits a closed-form solution. To evaluate the statistical performance of the proposed method, we conduct a series of numerical experiments using simulated data and gut microbiome data, which show that the proposed method achieves better estimation accuracy, competitive prediction performance, and more reliable outlier identification than the benchmark method RobRegCC.

title: Estimating the Effect of a Low Nicotine Standard on Smoking Behavior in the U.S. Population
comment: Joseph S. Koopmeiners and Jared D. Huling contributed equally to this work
summary: In January of 2025, the FDA announced a proposed rule to set a nationwide nicotine standard of 0.7 mg/cigarette that would reduce nicotine levels in cigarettes by 95$\%$. Past trials comparing very-low nicotine content (VLNC) cigarettes and normal nicotine content (NNC) cigarettes consistently found randomization to receive VLNC cigarettes reduces cigarette consumption. However, these results are not intrinsically generalizable, as the trials exhibited partial treatment non-adherence and were not designed as representative samples of the United States (U.S.) population of people who smoke (PWS). Existing transportability methods do not account for non-adherence or target a different estimand. Additionally, non-adherence cannot be directly observed and must be estimated using biomarkers of nicotine exposure, and different biomarkers were collected across trials. To estimate the effect of full adherence to a low nicotine standard in the U.S. population of PWS, we develop a novel inverse odds weighting estimator for transporting an intervention's effect to a fully adherent target population, and propose a bivariate mixture model approach for estimating adherence using biomarkers that allows partial missingness in one of the biomarkers. Finally, we use our method to transport inferences from seven trials investigating VLNC cigarettes to a representative sample of U.S. PWS.

title: An end-to-end framework for uncertainty-aware validation of generative models
summary: Density estimation with generative models is a common task in the physical sciences, for example in background estimation in particle physics. Existing machine learning techniques, however, lack methods to quantify uncertainties that can be propagated into a statistical test. That limits the validation of generative models to standard goodness-of-fit tests, in which the generative model is treated as exact (point-null hypothesis). But a model fitted to a finite training set is never exact, so if its uncertainties are neglected, any sufficiently powerful goodness-of-fit test will eventually reject it once the test set is large enough to resolve this estimation error. We propose SIGMA, an end-to-end framework combining density estimation with principled uncertainty quantification. We use Gaussian mixture models, for which uncertainties are tractable, and further construct a new goodness-of-fit test in which these uncertainties are profiled as nuisance parameters to account for the statistical error of the fit, promoting the conventional point-null test to a composite one. A rejection then signals genuine mismodeling rather than a test set large enough to resolve the error of the fit, provided the propagated uncertainties faithfully cover that error. We demonstrate the framework on a controlled two-dimensional toy model and on a collider physics benchmark modeling the QCD background process. With uncertainties included, the same model can be trusted on test sets up to an order of magnitude larger than the standard test allows. Our work thus provides a statistically grounded basis for a robust use of generative models in the physical sciences.

title: Bias-Aware Guardrail Selection Under Network Interference
summary: Web platforms use randomized experiment logs to choose budget-feasible treatment allocations while limiting losses to a designated group of units. Under network interference, each allocation requires expected outcomes at treatment-exposure pairs that may be sparsely observed. Existing safe policy selection methods require valid inference for each candidate, but pooling nearby exposures to improve estimability can introduce allocation-specific bias that variance-only bounds omit. We propose exposure-stratified guardrail selection (ESGuard), which aggregates unit-level bias bounds into a bias bound on each candidate's guardrail effect. It incorporates these bounds into simultaneous lower confidence bounds to select an allocation or retain the status quo. Under randomized rounds, a correct exposure mapping, and valid curvature and slope bounds, the conditional bias bound holds in finite samples. With independent rounds and additional regularity conditions, the unconditional probability of selecting an unsafe allocation is asymptotically at most the target level. We evaluate ESGuard on a simulator built from New York City ride-hailing trips. With six months of simulated rounds, we compare estimators that pool nearby exposures on the same logs and candidate sets. Adding the bias bound raises simultaneous coverage from below the nominal 95 percent level to at least 95 percent for every estimator in this comparison. In the underserved-only scenario, ESGuard violates the guardrail in 0.06 percent of its selections, compared with 16 percent for the point-estimate rule under the same gain ranking, and abstains in about a quarter of replications. Omitted spillovers can invalidate the protection. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/esguard-4D2E/.

title: Analysis of Uncertain GARCH Model with the application of crude oil future prices
summary: Time series data often exhibit variation, clustering, and persistence in uncertain environments. Based on an uncertain measure, existing studies have primarily focused on conditional mean structures while ignoring variance and persistent dynamics. To address this gap, this paper develops an uncertain generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (UGARCH) model that incorporates lagged conditional variance terms. We first prove sufficient conditions to ensure mean stationarity of the variance process. Then, we propose recursive constrained least squares to estimate the model parameters and use cross validation to determine the orders of the mean and variance equations. In addition, we also employ uncertain hypothesis tests to determine whether a time series exhibits a UGARCH effect and to assess the goodness of fit. Point and interval forecasts are subsequently constructed from the recursively obtained next-period conditional variance and the expected value of the mean equation. Numerical simulations demonstrate the parameter estimation performance of the proposed method and show that UGARCH achieves smaller conditional-variance fitting errors than UARCH under the considered settings. In the empirical analysis, we apply the proposed method to West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures closing prices, which exhibit time-varying volatility and support short-term point and interval forecasts. Keywords: Uncertain measure, Uncertain time-series analysis, UGARCH model, hypothesis test

title: Graph Representation Learning via Adaptive Expectile Aggregation
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) rely critically on neighborhood aggregation, yet conventional mean aggregation may fail to capture class-relevant distributional information, particularly in heterophilic graphs. We propose ExpectileGCN, an adaptive graph aggregation framework that introduces a learnable expectile level to capture neighborhood information beyond the mean. The proposed operator continuously adjusts aggregation between minimum- and maximum-type behaviors, with mean aggregation as a special case. A differentiable approximation based on sigmoid smoothing and fixed-point iterations enables end-to-end optimization. Theoretically, we establish stability properties and transductive generalization guarantees for ExpectileGCN. We further investigate its classification risk under heterophilic neighborhood models. For informative neighborhoods, we show that expectile aggregation can exploit class-dependent scale differences to achieve a classification advantage over mean aggregation. Under a local asymptotic regime with diminishing per-neighbor label informativeness, we establish that this advantage can persist in terms of limiting classification risk. Experiments on homophilic and heterophilic benchmark graphs demonstrate strong predictive performance and improved robustness under feature corruption and structural perturbations.

title: Neural Simulation-Based Inference for space-time Gaussian processes
summary: In spatio-temporal data analysis, estimating covariance parameters for Gaussian random fields via maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) is computationally prohibitive for large datasets. Following recent advances in simulation-based inference techniques, we propose two neural network architectures - Neural Bayes Estimation (NBE) and Neural Ratio Estimation (NRE) - to learn the parameters of Gaussian spatio-temporal Gneiting-Mat{é}rn models with advection. The networks are trained on simulations generated directly from the underlying Gaussian random field model. A thorough simulation study demonstrates strong performance across one-dimensional time and both one-dimensional space and two-dimensional space, yielding high accuracy and reliable uncertainty quantification for both NBE and NRE. Through extensive offline training, the framework achieves fully amortized inference, replacing costly optimization with a single forward pass. Finally, we apply our framework to solar radiation prediction and short-term forecasting. By adopting a sliding-window approach, the model accounts for temporal non-stationarity while retaining this key advantage: achieving near-instantaneous parameter inference and forecasting.

title: Is Your LLM Relay Serving What It Claims? A low-cost and high-power test for LLM Relay Auditing
summary: Relay and reseller APIs have become a common way to access large language models (LLMs), yet users cannot directly verify whether they receive the models they request and pay for. This opacity motivates LLM relay auditing, but existing methods struggle to combine low cost, robustness to benign deployment changes, and statistically interpretable decisions under black-box access. To address these limitations, we propose distributional fingerprint auditing (DFA), a statistical method that requires only textual responses from suspect and trusted reference endpoints. DFA repeatedly queries semantically simple finite-choice probes and uses the resulting categorical response distributions to construct endpoint fingerprints. It compares the suspect and reference fingerprints probe by probe and aggregates the resulting evidence using the Cauchy combination test, yielding an approximate endpoint-level $p$-value for audit decisions at a prespecified nominal significance level. Using registered fingerprints of candidate models, a likelihood-based formulation further supports model attribution under full substitution and joint estimation of substitute identity and substitution ratio under constant-ratio mixed routing. Our benchmark includes 16 proprietary and open-weight LLMs from 10 model families. Across 240 ordered full-substitution pairs, DFA achieves high detection rates at a nominal significance level of $α=0.05$, using five probes and 250 relay requests per audit with stored reference fingerprints. Configuration overrides can lead to rejection even when the served model remains unchanged, with effects varying across models and configurations. Simulations based on stored empirical fingerprints demonstrate accurate model attribution and estimate substitution ratios, with estimation error decreasing as the audit budget increases.

title: QD-PINN:A Physics-Informed Neural Network Approach to Bayesian Quickest Detection in High-Dimensional Diffusions
summary: Quickest detection problems (QDPs) arise in a wide range of applications. However, the complementarity structure of the associated variational inequalities poses substantial challenges for traditional numerical methods, particularly in high-dimensional settings. We propose a PINN-based framework for estimating the optimal stopping boundary in QDPs with high-dimensional diffusion processes and spatial dependence, while overcoming the curse of dimensionality. Theoretically, we establish a novel equivalence between the free-boundary PDE and an infinite-dimensional stochastic optimization problem, rigorously justifying the use of finite-dimensional neural networks to approximate the true solution. Furthermore, we assess the robustness of the proposed framework by quantifying uncertainty in the learned stopping boundaries using deep ensembles and Monte Carlo dropout. The results show low variability across independent training runs and stochastic forward passes, indicating stable and consistent boundary estimates. We also compare our PINN results with reference numerical solutions where available and find close agreement.

title: Estimation and Inference for One-pass Streaming Function-on-Function Regression
summary: In many applications, functional pairs are collected sequentially from a data stream. Existing function-on-function regression methods are primarily designed for batch data, and bootstrap inference has become one of the most popular approaches. However, this procedure may be infeasible when observations cannot be stored. In this paper, we propose a one-pass functional SGD estimator that updates upon each observation's arrival without data storage, and a weighted rolling validation rule is provided for step size selection for implementation. Further, an online multiplier bootstrap is developed for inference that updates perturbed stochastic gradient paths in parallel, bypassing estimating an infinite-dimensional covariance operator. Asymptotic behaviors are established for the proposed method, and conditional bootstrap validity is justified for the bias-centered pointwise estimation error. Simulation studies and two real data applications confirm the empirical effectiveness of the proposed procedures. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first theoretically justified one-pass framework for bootstrap inference on a bivariate coefficient surface with streaming functional data.

title: Bayesian Ordinal Analysis of Cereal Growth Stage Data from Oat Trials in Western Australia
comment: 34 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables; supplementary material with 5 figures and 12 tables
summary: Growth stage in cereal field trials is usually scored on the Zadoks decimal scale. The score is ordinal, yet it is often analysed as if it were continuous, which can lead to misleading conclusions. Ordinal analysis of growth stage data has received little attention from biometricians or agronomists, and it is not straightforward when several plants are scored in each plot of a split-plot design. We analysed Zadoks scores recorded four weeks after sowing on ten plants per plot in two deep-sowing oat trials in Western Australia, using a Bayesian hierarchical ordinal model that carries the full split-plot structure and an AR1 x AR1 spatial covariance. The implementation was validated on simulated data, and the candidate models were compared by five-fold cross-validation over plots. Adding a random effect at the experimental-unit (plot) level changed the uncertainty of the sub-plot contrasts substantially, while the main-plot contrasts changed little. How that plot-level heterogeneity was modelled mattered much less. At either site, cross-validation could not separate the candidate models that carried a plot-level term, whether or not they included an AR1 x AR1 field or the blocking terms, and the autoregressive parameters were only weakly identified on this layout. Deeper sowing (80 and 120 mm against 30 mm) went with more advanced development at four weeks in both trials. Sowing at 120 mm rather than 30 mm raised the predicted probability of tillering from 0.04 to 0.24 at Wickepin and from 0.04 to 0.10 at Merredin. The depth effects were stable whether or not the spatial field was fitted, and under both the cumulative and the sequential ordinal family.

title: Directional Statistics on Circles and Spheres: A New Angle on Data
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures. Expository article with real-data examples and reproducible R code. Submitted to Resonance: Journal of Science Education
summary: Two compass bearings near north can have an ordinary arithmetic mean pointing south: the difficulty is that angles live on a circle, not a straight line. Using real wind observations, diffusion-MRI orientations, and geometric examples from machine learning, this article introduces circular and axial averages, directional variability, and probability models on circles and spheres. The guiding principle is to identify the geometry and symmetries of the observations before choosing a statistical method.

title: Efficient Bootstrap Calibration of Generalized Posteriors with Importance Reweighting
summary: The learning rate of a generalized posterior governs posterior uncertainty but typically has no canonical value. Generalized posterior calibration (GPC) selects this rate by matching bootstrap-estimated credible-interval coverage to its nominal level, often requiring repeated posterior simulation. We propose GPC via importance reweighting (GPC-IRW), which reuses draws from a reference posterior fitted to the original data across bootstrap resamples and candidate learning rates. For quantile-based intervals of a scalar functional, we express the coverage criterion in terms of bootstrap posterior cumulative distribution functions, avoiding computation of individual bootstrap credible intervals. Safeguards based on importance-weight effective sample size and proximity to coverage-decision boundaries invoke reweighting from cached bootstrap-specific draws or direct posterior simulation when necessary. Under the stated regularity conditions, with numerical error tending to zero, we show that median-centered calibration preserves the first-order learning-rate target and achieves asymptotically nominal coverage. The approach extends to independent clusters through cluster-level resampling. Simulations yield coverage and interval lengths comparable to those of existing GPC algorithms at substantially lower computational cost. In an exoplanet mass-radius analysis, GPC-IRW achieves 6.7- and 9.6-fold speedups over MCMC-based calibration in the single-planet and full-sample analyses, respectively, while illustrating the effects of within-host dependence.

title: Priors and parameterizations for Bayesian regression with categorical variables and interactions
summary: Regression analysis commonly features categorical variables and their interactions to model heterogeneous, group-specific effects. Such interactions are notorious for weak signals and cumbersome parameterizations, and thus urgently require shrinkage. However, the overwhelming default for linear models--using dummy coding, removing a reference group, and applying shrinkage--leads to unwelcome biases, asymmetries, and parameter incongruities across models. We resolve these limitations with a new parameterization-prior combination that couples abundance-based constraints for identifiability with customized shrinkage priors for categorical effects and interactions (BayesABCs). BayesABCs offers a surprising and unique invariance property: the joint posterior of all main effects is (nearly) unchanged by the addition of categorical interactions. We show how this, in conjunction with our shrinkage priors, effectively removes the principal drawbacks of including categorical interactions, thereby making heterogeneous effect estimation broadly feasible. We enforce the identifiability constraints via conditioning and provide a model representation that facilitates efficient posterior computing and direct analysis. Across simulations with a variety of categorical effects and interactions, BayesABCs consistently produces more accurate estimates and predictions, sharper inferences, and unmatched robustness to extraneous interactions relative to competing parameterizations and priors. We apply BayesABCs to study disparities in the error rates of automatic speech recognition systems.

title: Wasserstein approximation of measures via orthogonal frames: statistical and computational complexities
summary: Dimension-reduction methods such as PCA identify a subspace capturing most of the variation in the data, but not a distinguished basis within it. Selecting a basis in which the samples are sparsely represented is a recurring task in unsupervised learning, addressed by methods in factor analysis, dictionary learning, and subspace clustering. We pose this task as Wasserstein approximation of the data distribution by measures supported on the axes of an orthogonal frame, which, in turn, reduces to a nonsmooth optimization problem over the orthogonal group $\mathrm{O}(d)$. We show that, under mild assumptions, both empirical risk minimizers and a locally initialized stochastic gradient method recover the population-optimal frame at the near-parametric rate $\widetilde{O}_d(n^{-1/2})$, where $n$ is the sample size. The main difficulty is that, although the population objective is smooth, the empirical objective is not-this mismatch precludes standard covering arguments. We overcome this issue by replacing Lipschitz continuity of the empirical gradient with a coarsely Lipschitz bound, a tool that may be of independent interest. Numerical experiments support our theoretical findings.

title: Penalized Cause-Specific Hazard Regression under Competing Risks: An Elastic Net Approach Using SANAD Trial Data
summary: Competing risks analysis is an important framework for studying time-to-event data in the presence of multiple, mutually exclusive events. Traditional methods, such as non-parametric estimators and proportional hazards models, may not adequately capture complex hazard patterns or provide stable estimates in practical settings. In this study, we propose a parametric approach based on the generalized exponential regression model for competing risks data. The model allows flexible hazard shapes and incorporates covariate effects through a regression structure. To improve estimation stability, we integrate elastic net regularization into the likelihood framework. The proposed method is evaluated through simulation studies and applied to a real dataset. The results indicate that the elastic net approach provides more stable and precise estimates compared to standard maximum likelihood estimation. Overall, the proposed framework offers a flexible and practical approach for analyzing competing risks data.

title: Finite-population inference for cross-fitted estimators of treatment contrasts in stratified multistage surveys
comment: 30 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables; 41-page supplementary appendix included as an ancillary file. Reproduction materials: https://github.com/ehsanx/svycf-reproducibility
summary: Health surveys often sample clusters within strata and then individuals within clusters, and flexible outcome and treatment models complicate inference for adjusted contrasts from such surveys. We establish finite-population limit theory for survey-weighted augmented inverse-probability-weighted estimation within the double machine learning framework, using cross-fitting that keeps whole clusters together; a cross-fitted targeted maximum likelihood estimator inherits the results under additional targeting conditions. With first-stage clusters drawn by simple random sampling without replacement within strata, the theory allows arbitrary within-cluster dependence, appreciable sampling fractions, and many small strata, a few large strata, or both. Under bounded cluster sizes, a cluster-generation model and nuisance convergence-rate conditions, the estimator is asymptotically normal about the finite-population contrast, and a stability property derived from the cluster model controls the cross-fitting error without entropy conditions. The stratified ultimate-cluster variance estimator, without a first-stage finite-population correction, consistently estimates a with-replacement variance that is at least the without-replacement design variance of the normal limit, so the resulting intervals are asymptotically conservative, and exact when the excess is negligible. In simulations, near-nominal or higher coverage coexisted, in different settings, with remainder diagnostics above the study's negligibility benchmark and with inaccurate standard errors. In three Service Provision Assessment surveys from Malawi and Haiti, each frame treated as a fixed population and resampled 500 times, mean reported standard errors were 4%-20% larger than the empirical standard deviations, while coverage of whole-frame reference values was near or above nominal.

title: Cost-based variable selection for prediction models
comment: 43 pages, 3 main figures, 4 main tables, 12 supplementary figures, 4 supplementary tables
summary: Objective: Variable selection for clinical prediction models is commonly done on statistical grounds related to model fit. Statistical approaches ignore the cost of misclassifications and the harm of measuring a variable. We aim to develop a decision-analytic variable selection algorithm based on net benefit. Materials and Methods: The proposed algorithm selects the set of predictors by exhaustively comparing the net benefit of all combinations using cross validation, with an extension based on backward elimination for settings with many predictors. Variables are selected if the increased net benefit from better predictiveness exceeds the net benefit reduction from the harm of variable measurement. title: When Scatter Plots Hide the Data: Diagnosing Ties and Choosing the Right Display in R
summary: Scatter plots draw one mark per observation, so observations that share a location are hidden. In a two-item Likert survey of 2,757 respondents, 98.7% of the data lie under other points and the plot shows only 36 dots. The density-distribution sunflower plot of Dupont and Plummer addresses this by drawing raw points in sparse regions and sunflowers, whose petals count observations, in dense ones. It is not available in R, and its single petal weight for dense cells fails when cell counts span more than an order of magnitude: small dense cells collapse to one petal, and the count a reader decodes can be wrong by 150% or more. We propose geometric petal tiers, in which each cell uses the smallest weight among 1, b, b2, . . . observations per petal that keeps its flower within P petals. Every flower then has between about P/b and P petals, and the relative error of every decoded count is below b/(2P), 17.9% at the defaults b = 5 and P = 14. We also define tie diagnostics and decision rules that use them to choose between an ordinary scatter plot, jitter or transparency, a classic sunflower plot and geometric tiers. Both are implemented in the ggplot2 extension ggsunflower. We illustrate the methods on survey, automotive, historical and large commercial data, and in a simulation over 35 conditions geometric tiers keep the worst-cell error at or below 14% where a single weight reaches a median of 251%.

title: Practical Guidelines for Goodness-of-Fit Testing for Right-Censored Data
summary:
In survival studies, right censoring often prevents the observation of subjects' complete outcomes, complicating inference about the underlying distribution. Evaluating whether a given distribution adequately fits right-censored data is therefore essential. However, guidance on the relative performance of available goodness-of-fit tests under different data conditions remains limited.
  In this work, we present a comparative assessment of three classical goodness-of-fit tests adapted for right-censored data: Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling, and Cramér-von Mises. Through an extensive simulation study, we investigate how factors such as the proportion of right-censored observations, sample size, and distributional symmetry influence the statistical power of each test.
  All procedures were implemented using the R package GofCens, and power estimates were obtained from extensive replicated simulations. The results identify the settings in which each test exhibits superior performance, providing practical, evidence-based recommendations for test selection in survival analysis. These recommendations are summarized as user-oriented guidelines and complemented by a concise graphical cheat sheet, enabling practitioners to quickly identify the most suitable test for their specific application.

title: Penalized Cause-Specific Hazard Regression under Competing Risks: An Elastic Net Approach Using SANAD Trial Data
summary: Competing risks analysis is an important framework for studying time-to-event data in the presence of multiple, mutually exclusive events. Traditional methods, such as non-parametric estimators and proportional hazards models, may not adequately capture complex hazard patterns or provide stable estimates in practical settings. In this study, we propose a parametric approach based on the generalized exponential regression model for competing risks data. The model allows flexible hazard shapes and incorporates covariate effects through a regression structure. To improve estimation stability, we integrate elastic net regularization into the likelihood framework. The proposed method is evaluated through simulation studies and applied to a real dataset. The results indicate that the elastic net approach provides more stable and precise estimates compared to standard maximum likelihood estimation. Overall, the proposed framework offers a flexible and practical approach for analyzing competing risks data.

title: Agentic Distributional Regression: Conditional Density Estimation through Agent-Written Programs
summary: In this paper we propose a method for estimating conditional densities from an iid sample using a language-model agent. The agent writes the estimator as a short program that, for each covariate value, returns the estimated conditional distribution of the response. The program is built from a library of probability distributions, so the returned law can be a parametric distribution, a mixture or a multivariate factorization, with parameters given by explicit functions of the covariates. Since the number of operations and constants in the program is limited, the fitted conditional density is a formula that can be inspected and evaluated independently of the agent, while the choice of the model structure and of the fitting procedure is left to the agent. We call this approach agentic distributional regression (ADR). Treating the returned program as a random conditional density estimator, we derive a finite-sample error bound under explicit complexity and optimization assumptions, and an oracle inequality for selection using independent validation data. For a stably selected regular structure with sufficiently accurate fitting, we obtain asymptotic normality of the fitted constants. In simulation studies, on twelve real datasets and on a new dataset collected after the agents' training data, ADR with Claude Opus 5.5 has the best average performance among the methods considered.

title: A flexible approach to high-dimensional clustering and classification using mixtures of finite mutually repulsive mixtures
summary: We propose a novel approach for clustering that is later extended to classification. Our methods are based on an underlying determinantal point process (DPP) that generates sparsity and separation of location parameters in a mixture of finite mixture models specification. A key aspect is the assumption of a DPP conditional on the number of groups and a prior on this number, which results in a dynamic mixture of repulsive mixtures. The proposed model also involves a sparse tensor decomposition of the covariance function used to define the DPP, which is coupled with a separate mixture model employed to handle the intra-cluster correlation structure. Further computational enhancement in the high-dimensional case comes from exploiting a mapping from Euclidean space to the space of (valid) correlation matrices. A suitable posterior simulation scheme involving a modified telescopic sampler is developed. The resulting approach is seen to perform satisfactorily in simulated and real data examples.

title: Causal sensitivity analyses for indirect and spillover mediation effects in cluster-randomized trials: Application to a pragmatic trial on chronic pain management
summary: Causal mediation in cluster-randomized trials can clarify whether a cluster-level intervention changes patient outcomes through patient- and peer-level processes, but identification relies on untestable cross-world assumptions. We develop a two-part sensitivity analysis for violations of two distinct cross-world independence assumptions. The first component adapts bridge score sensitivity analysis to assess residual mediator-outcome confounding with clustered mediator exposures; the second uses a Gaussian copula to assess cross-world dependence between an individual's treated mediator and summaries of control-arm peer mediators. The resulting framework parameterizes unidentifiable dependence structures using interpretable correlation parameters and combines them with a flexible Bayesian nonparametric model to characterize the plausible range of the target estimands. A nested common-atoms enriched Dirichlet process models the observed data and supports posterior-predictive standardization. We apply the framework to the Pain Program for Active Coping and Training trial, a primary care-embedded cognitive behavioral therapy intervention for adults with chronic pain receiving long-term opioid therapy. The intervention had a negative total effect on twelve-month pain-related disability. The natural indirect and direct effect decomposition was sensitive to plausible directional residual confounding, whereas the spillover and individual mediation effect decomposition changed little across the copula sensitivity analyses and attributed most of the negative indirect signal to the individual's mediator. Jointly relaxing both assumptions substantially increased uncertainty about the pathways. The analysis supports an overall improvement in disability and a plausible individual pain-impact pathway, while showing that detailed mechanistic claims remain assumption-dependent.

title: CircaFMM: A Flexible Statistical Framework for Circadian Rhythmicity Detection in Transcriptomics
comment: Supplementary Data 1 and 2 are available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request
summary: Detecting circadian rhythmicity in large-scale transcriptomic data is challenging when sampling is irregular, signals are weak, and expression profiles deviate from sinusoidal shapes. The fixed harmonic form of classical Cosinor-based methods may therefore be poorly suited to asymmetric and temporally complex rhythms. We present CircaFMM, a flexible framework for circadian rhythmicity detection based on the single-component Frequency Modulated Möbius (FMM) model. CircaFMM defines rhythmicity as time dependence induced by the Möbius phase parameter, so that the non-rhythmic null corresponds to a time-invariant mean profile. The resulting non-regular test combines time-density weighting, regularized estimation, and bootstrap calibration of a weighted likelihood-ratio-type statistic. Simulations showed controlled type-I error under irregular sampling and improved power over the classical Cosinor F-test for asymmetric waveforms. Applied to the GTEx-13T postmortem transcriptomic dataset, CircaFMM recovered canonical clock genes and circadian pathways while identifying additional rhythmic candidates with lower signal-to-noise-ratio, greater waveform asymmetry, and non-sinusoidal temporal profiles. CircaFMM is available at https://circafmm.shinyapps.io/circafmm_shinyapp/, with source code at https://github.com/FMMGroupVa/CircaFMM.

title: Bayesian Recovery Trajectories Following Forced Sexual Experience: Healthcare Access and Social Support Among Women
comment: Submitted to Social Psychiatry and Psychiatric Epidemiology
summary:
\textbf{Background.} Women who experience forced sexual violence face elevated risks of poor mental and physical health, but whether long-term health follows distinct trajectories and whether healthcare access and social support differentiate them remains unclear.
  \textbf{Methods.} We analyzed 1,848 women from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), followed from adolescence into adulthood. An identified Bayesian mixture model classified joint mental and physical health burden trajectories from six repeated indicators. Bayesian logistic models estimated associations of forced sexual experience, healthcare access, social support, and demographics with trajectory membership. Robustness was assessed across three mixture specifications and four- and five-class alternatives.
  \textbf{Results.} We retained three classes: low-burden/resilient (27.2\% posterior mean weight), moderate/worsening burden (43.2\%), and high chronic burden (29.7\%). All specifications converged ($\hat{R}=1.00$) with well-separated classes; four- and five-class alternatives had convergence problems or an unstable additional class. Forced sexual experience was associated with higher posterior odds of high chronic burden (OR = 3.78, 95\% credible interval [CrI] 2.84--5.04) and moderate/worsening burden (OR = 1.63, 95\% CrI 1.26--2.12). Better healthcare access and greater social connectedness were independently associated with lower posterior odds of high chronic burden.
  \noindent\textbf{Conclusions.} Long-term health after forced sexual experience follows heterogeneous trajectories. Healthcare access and social connectedness distinguish more favorable trajectories and represent modifiable targets for trauma-informed, longitudinal, survivor-centered care.

title: Close Races and Similarity Bias: A Bayesian Analysis of the Ranked Ballots for the Ballon d'Or
summary: The Ballon d'Or ranks players whose contributions have no common unit, so its results are often disputed. Regressions of award points describe associations but not how complete ballots arise or how likely a different winner would be. We propose a Bayesian mixture-of-experts model for partial rankings that learns nonlinear performance relationships, the number of voting styles and journalists' style memberships. A shared soft regression tree with style-specific leaf values lets styles evaluate the same season records differently on a common basis. Region-dependent mixing probabilities and journalist--nominee similarity terms separate geographic differences in voting styles from affinity within a style, and journalist- and rank-specific precisions capture remaining variation. We establish identification and consistency for the number of occupied styles under explicit conditions; simulations examine recovery, calibration and robustness to misspecification. Applied to all 176 published ballots from 2019 and 99 from 2024, the model compares award outcomes under changes in affinity and jury composition. For 2019, Messi's probability of winning with a new jury from the same countries rises from 0.49 to 0.76 when similarity terms are removed. For 2024, the direction of this change depends on whether affinities differ by region. Regional representation changes winner probabilities more than jury size.

title: Joint Distributional Copula Regression for Insurance Claim Frequency and Severity via Boosting
summary: In this paper, we propose a model-based boosting approach for fitting structured additive distributional copula regression models with bivariate responses, focusing particularly on the joint modeling of claim frequency and claim severity. The proposed approach is based on generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS), which extend the general idea of GAMs by allowing multiple parameters of a response distribution, rather than only its conditional mean, to depend on covariates. The model is therefore intrinsically interpretable at the level of its additive predictors, providing greater transparency and auditability than black-box alternatives. We evaluate the proposed framework using synthetic and real-world data. We demonstrate its ability to recover the underlying covariate effects and dependence structure, identify informative variables, and achieve competitive predictive performance relative to benchmark models. We also illustrate how the fitted model can be interpreted.

title: Reducing Complexity of Pseudo-Marginal Sequential Monte Carlo via Hierarchical Tempering
summary: The Bayesian approach to inverse problems provides a powerful framework for inferring unknown parameters from noisy observations. Among the computationally most challenging statistical inference problems are problems with intractable likelihoods, especially if no unbiased likelihood estimator is available. We focus on a class of such problems, where a biased likelihood estimator is obtained through a stochastic approximation of a forward map (stochastic solver). Obtaining an empirical posterior approximation in applications is very expensive due to the repeated stochastic solver evaluations required by standard sampling methods. To address this computational bottleneck, we develop a novel algorithm based on a density-tempered marginalized Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampler. Our approach (hierarchical SMC) accelerates inference by leveraging a hierarchy of stochastic solvers with increasing accuracy both along the tempering sequence and within mutation stages of the SMC sampler. We establish, under additional assumptions, that the asymptotic speedup is proportional to the number of tempering stages $T$. We demonstrate computational gains on several examples, including a nonlinear, high-contrast inverse problem arising in photoacoustic medical imaging. On this problem, we demonstrate a speedup by a factor of 14.3, reducing the inference wall-clock time from about 4.6 days to 7.7 hours on an NVIDIA A40 GPU.
